white-sheet:
## What this is

The calibration sheet for the Breach triptych's paper stack. Three tabloid sheets (279.4 x 431.8 mm) are plotted, knife-cut, trimmed at the crop marks, stacked flat and glued: white paper at the back (the bottom), gold-yellow paper over it, black paper in front (the top). The black sheet has big windows (W1 upper left, W2 upper right) that show the gold sheet, and the gold sheet has a window (G1, inside W2) that shows the white sheet. The lower half of the front sheet is plain black paper. This sheet is only a test: it is not signed, and none of it is art.

It measures, before the real triptych is drawn:

- the real line width of each ink on each paper, and which inks read on which paper;
- how legible the cut guides are;
- how close art can sit to a knife cut (the margin);
- how far lower art must run under an upper edge (the bleed);
- how far apart the sheets register after trimming at the crop marks, read to 0.1 mm with verniers;
- whether ink on the white sheet ghosts through the gold-yellow paper over it (nothing ghosts through the black paper in front).

## This sheet: white paper (the back ply)

Plot on white paper with the four Microns (01 black, 08 black, 05 blue and 05 purple), and, on trial on white, the Signo 1.0mm silver and the Moonlight 10 fl pink and fl orange. It has no cuts: trim it at the crop marks and it is done. Window G1 (in the gold sheet) shows the swatches of the seven inks (one column: the four Microns, then silver, fl pink and fl orange on trial), the bleed ladder toward G1's bottom edge and the labels of the main scales for the gold-over-white verniers. Everything else lies under the gold and black papers and is sealed once the stack is glued, so read it on the loose sheet before gluing: the one-line title along the top edge, the main scales of the two G verniers, the font test (right, in the lower half), the spacing ladder (upper left), the marks ladder (dots and dashes), the ink crossings, an edge ruler at the middle of each side, and the carbon ghost-test hatch box (a Micron 01 hatch 40 x 14 mm, x 88 to 128 and y 160 to 174), which sits under the gold inside W1. The font test, spacing ladder, marks ladder and crossings carry all seven of the white's inks.

## Pens, in plot order

The dashboard asks for each layer by its id. Every test on the sheet is labelled, in its own ink, with the name of the pen that should have drawn it: a label in the wrong colour means the wrong pen was fitted for that layer.

1. `carbon`: Micron 01 black
2. `black`: Micron 08 black
3. `ultramarine`: Micron 05 blue
4. `violet`: Micron 05 purple
5. `silver`: Signo 1.0mm silver
6. `fluoro-pink`: Moonlight 10 fl pink
7. `fluoro-orange`: Moonlight 10 fl orange
8. `finishing-border`: Micron 01 black (crop marks)

## Plot, cut and assemble

1. Plot all three sheets (white, gold and black) on their own paper, white first, then gold, then black, one pen layer after another in the order of the pen plan, without moving the paper. Gel inks marked "(trial)" are being tried on that paper for the first time. Real plot time runs about three times finalize's estimate: roughly 45 minutes for the white sheet, 35 for the gold-yellow and 1 hour for the black, about 2 h 20 min for the three, plus the pen swaps.
2. Let the gel ink dry at least 1 hour before cutting.
3. Cut each sheet's windows along the **outer edge** of the drawn outline (the knife goes on the line the outline just touches). White sheet: no windows. Gold sheet: G1, and the cut ladder in its lower left. Black sheet: W1, W2 and the five small windows A, B, C, D and E (E is the margin-ladder window).
4. Trim every sheet at its crop marks.
5. Before gluing, read everything sealed on the white and gold sheets (see What to read). Then stack flat, bottom to top: white, gold, black, squared in an L-square against the same corner. Glue the gold sheet onto the white, then the black onto the gold.

## What to read

- **Ink swatches** (each ink on its own paper): a 22 x 12 mm hatch patch at 0.6 mm pitch; beside it a single line, a dashed line and a 3 mm hatch strip at 0.3 mm pitch. Where the strip fuses to solid the line is wider than 0.3 mm. The white's seven are in G1 (one column), the gold's in W1 (two columns), the black's thirteen in four columns in the lower half. For each ink on each paper say whether it **reads**, is **weak** or **does not read**, and the single line's width if you can measure it.
- **Cut-guide variants** (black sheet, windows A to D, plotted before cutting): the X marks and label differ in pitch and size (A pitch 12, size 4; B pitch 8, size 3; C pitch 16, size 6; D no label). Say which is the **smallest variant that is still obvious** to cut by.
- **Margin ladder** (black sheet beside window E, gold sheet above window G1): four lines at 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm from the cut line. After cutting, find the line closest to the cut that the knife **spared** (whole, not nicked or cut away). That offset is the working margin.
- **Bleed ladder** (gold sheet at the bottom edge of W1, white sheet at the bottom edge of G1): seven lines that end -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 mm past the edge (negative: they stop short, inside the window). The gold ladder runs under the black, the white one under the gold. After assembly, find the **shortest line that shows no gap** at the edge. That offset is the working bleed.
- **Ghost** (one box): a Micron 01 carbon hatch on the white sheet, 40 x 14 mm, lies under the gold-yellow paper inside W1. On the gold sheet, in black ink over it, is the caption "is there a ghost here?". Say whether the hatch shows through the gold-yellow paper (read it through W1, after gluing). Nothing ghosts through the black paper in front, so there is no second box.
- **Font test** (each sheet, each of its inks; black: Signo gold, silver and Moonlight 10 fl pink only; white: all seven inks): the word "line" in the Hershey sans face and then in the script face, at 1.5, 2.0, 2.6, 3.5 and 5 mm (cap height), left to right on one baseline, and below them "everything falls into line" in sans at 2.6 mm, the size the triptych's phrase is drawn at (on the art each word rides one of the lines, in that line's ink). For each ink on each paper find the **smallest size that is still legible** at arm's length, in sans and in script, and say whether the 2.6 mm phrase reads. The white sheet's font test is sealed under the gold and black: read it before gluing. The gold's is in view in W1, and the black's in the lower half.
- **Spacing ladder** (each sheet; white: all seven inks, sealed; gold: its five inks, hidden under the black; black: Signo gold, silver and Moonlight 10 fl pink): 5 x 5 mm hatch patches at 0.40, 0.50, 0.55, 0.66, 0.80 and 1.00 mm between line centres, then a 3 mm square outlined twice and three times at 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 1.0 and 1.2 mm. Find the **tightest spacing whose lines stay separate** (not fused to solid), for hatch, doubles and triples.
- **Dots, dashes and tight curves** (each sheet, each ink as above): dash rows 0.3, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.6 mm on with gaps as long; a row of dots, three each of strokes 0.3, 0.35 and 0.4 mm long; crosses 0.8, 1.2 and 1.6 mm across (the sizes of the stars); circles of radius 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 mm; a spiral from 2 to 8 mm across. Find the **shortest dash** and the **smallest circle** that draw cleanly without skipping, and say whether the dots show. Two things the pipeline does, so they are expected: the 0.3 mm dashes come out as one line (finalize joins strokes whose ends are under 0.4 mm apart before the plotter gets them), and a true point never reaches the plotter (the render drops zero-length strokes and finalize any shorter than 0.3 mm), so the dots are the shortest strokes that do.
- **Ink crossings** (black sheet: Signo gold, silver and Moonlight 10 fl pink; white sheet, sealed: all seven inks; the gold sheet has none): every pair of inks crosses twice, the row's ink across and the column's ink down. The pen plotted later is on top, in the sheet's plot order (see Pens): on the black silver, then fl pink, then gold; on the white carbon (Micron 01), Micron 08, blue, purple, silver, fl pink, fl orange. Say whether any crossing **smears or drags** the earlier ink, and if you plot a sheet a second time with a pause between pens (10 minutes or so), whether waiting helps.
- **Cut ladder** (gold sheet, lower left; cut it with G1, before gluing; its labels are hidden under the black): wedges whose tips close to 60, 45, 30 and 20 degrees; slots 3, 4, 5 and 6 mm wide and 30 long; three windows round a kept island held by one bridge 2, 3 or 4 mm wide (as the shirt cut holds the tie at its knot and tip); a notch open to the bottom trim. Find the **sharpest wedge** whose tip cuts clean, the **narrowest slot** that cuts clean, the **narrowest bridge** that holds its island, and whether the notch cuts clean at the trim.
- **Edge rulers** (each sheet, the middle of each side; the white's and gold's are hidden once glued): four short lines 12, 13, 14 and 16 mm from the paper edge, labelled, that is 1, 2, 3 and 5 mm inside the crop line (all art is clipped to the crop line, so the margin itself cannot carry lines). Before trimming, measure with a rule from the paper edge to the 12 line on each side: the difference from 12 mm is how far the plot landed from where it was placed on the bed.
- **Verniers** (read to 0.1 mm, with a loupe): there are four, two per neighbouring pair of sheets. Black over gold at W1 and gold over white at G1 each have an **x** vernier on the window's bottom edge (it reads left-right registration) and a **y** vernier on its right edge (it reads up-down registration). Each has a main scale of 21 ticks at 1.00 mm on the lower sheet (10 mm either side of its 0 tick, every fifth tick longer, running 4 mm under the upper paper; on the gold in black ink for W1, on the white in carbon for G1) and a vernier of 11 ticks at 0.90 mm on the upper sheet's paper, starting at the edge (on the black in silver for W1, on the gold in black ink for G1). The two 0 ticks line up when registration is perfect. The main scales of the G verniers are on the white, under the gold: read them on the loose sheet before gluing, or through G1 after.
  - Find the vernier tick that continues in a straight line across the cut into a main-scale tick. Call its number k: 0 is the vernier's first tick, 10 its last, ticks 5 and 10 are longer.
  - The main-scale tick at or just before the vernier's 0 tick, counted from the main 0 tick, gives the whole millimetres, n. The vernier tick k that lines up gives the tenths.
  - Reading = n + 0.1 x k mm. The arrow marked + is the positive direction: positive means the upper sheet sits further right (x) or further down (y) than the lower one. Example: the vernier's 0 tick falls just past the main 0 tick and its tick 3 lines up: +0.3 mm. If the vernier's 0 tick falls just before the main 0 tick, n is -1: with tick 7 lined up the reading is -1 + 0.7 = -0.3 mm. The tenths can be read for shifts from about -10 mm to +2 mm; beyond that, report just the whole millimetres.

## Report back

- Line width per ink per paper: reads / weak / no (and the width of the single line if you can measure it).
- The smallest cut-guide variant (A, B, C or D) that is still obvious.
- The margin line the knife spared (0.5, 1.0, 1.5 or 2.0 mm), on the black and on the gold sheet.
- The gap-free bleed line (its label in mm), on the gold ladder (through W1) and the white one (through G1).
- The x and y vernier readings for each pair: black over gold (at W1) and gold over white (at G1). Note whether you read them before or after gluing.
- Whether the ghost shows (the carbon hatch through the gold-yellow paper).
- Font test: the smallest legible size per ink per paper, sans and script (1.5, 2.0, 2.6, 3.5 or 5 mm), and whether the 2.6 mm phrase reads in each ink (above all Moonlight 10 fl pink on white, Signo gold on black and the Micron blacks on gold-yellow: the inks the phrase is drawn in).
- Spacing ladder: the tightest separate spacing per ink per paper, for hatch, doubles and triples.
- Dots, dashes and curves: the shortest clean dash and the smallest clean circle per ink per paper, and whether the dots show.
- Crossings: any smear or drag (which pair, which way), and whether a pause between pens helps.
- Cut ladder: the sharpest clean wedge, the narrowest clean slot, the narrowest bridge that held, and the notch.
- Edge rulers: the measured distance from the paper edge to the 12 mm line on each side (top, bottom, left, right), per sheet.

Nothing is plotted or cut until you say go.

4. Trim every sheet at its crop marks.
5. Before gluing, read everything sealed on the white and gold sheets (see What to read). Then stack flat, bottom to top: white, gold, black, squared in an L-square against the same corner. Glue the gold sheet onto the white, then the black onto the gold.

## What to read

- **Ink swatches** (each ink on its own paper): a 22 x 12 mm hatch patch at 0.6 mm pitch; beside it a single line, a dashed line and a 3 mm hatch strip at 0.3 mm pitch. Where the strip fuses to solid the line is wider than 0.3 mm. The white's seven are in G1 (one column), the gold's in W1 (two columns), the black's thirteen in four columns in the lower half. For each ink on each paper say whether it **reads**, is **weak** or **does not read**, and the single line's width if you can measure it.
- **Cut-guide variants** (black sheet, windows A to D, plotted before cutting): the X marks and label differ in pitch and size (A pitch 12, size 4; B pitch 8, size 3; C pitch 16, size 6; D no label). Say which is the **smallest variant that is still obvious** to cut by.
- **Margin ladder** (black sheet beside window E, gold sheet above window G1): four lines at 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm from the cut line. After cutting, find the line closest to the cut that the knife **spared** (whole, not nicked or cut away). That offset is the working margin.
- **Bleed ladder** (gold sheet at the bottom edge of W1, white sheet at the bottom edge of G1): seven lines that end -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 mm past the edge (negative: they stop short, inside the window). The gold ladder runs under the black, the white one under the gold. After assembly, find the **shortest line that shows no gap** at the edge. That offset is the working bleed.
- **Ghost** (one box): a Micron 01 carbon hatch on the white sheet, 40 x 14 mm, lies under the gold-yellow paper inside W1. On the gold sheet, in black ink over it, is the caption "is there a ghost here?". Say whether the hatch shows through the gold-yellow paper (read it through W1, after gluing). Nothing ghosts through the black paper in front, so there is no second box.
- **Font test** (each sheet, each of its inks; black: Signo gold, silver and Moonlight 10 fl pink only; white: all seven inks): the word "line" in the Hershey sans face and then in the script face, at 1.5, 2.0, 2.6, 3.5 and 5 mm (cap height), left to right on one baseline, and below them "everything falls into line" in sans at 2.6 mm, the size the triptych's phrase is drawn at (on the art each word rides one of the lines, in that line's ink). For each ink on each paper find the **smallest size that is still legible** at arm's length, in sans and in script, and say whether the 2.6 mm phrase reads. The white sheet's font test is sealed under the gold and black: read it before gluing. The gold's is in view in W1, and the black's in the lower half.
- **Spacing ladder** (each sheet; white: all seven inks, sealed; gold: its five inks, hidden under the black; black: Signo gold, silver and Moonlight 10 fl pink): 5 x 5 mm hatch patches at 0.40, 0.50, 0.55, 0.66, 0.80 and 1.00 mm between line centres, then a 3 mm square outlined twice and three times at 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 1.0 and 1.2 mm. Find the **tightest spacing whose lines stay separate** (not fused to solid), for hatch, doubles and triples.
- **Dots, dashes and tight curves** (each sheet, each ink as above): dash rows 0.3, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.6 mm on with gaps as long; a row of dots, three each of strokes 0.3, 0.35 and 0.4 mm long; crosses 0.8, 1.2 and 1.6 mm across (the sizes of the stars); circles of radius 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 mm; a spiral from 2 to 8 mm across. Find the **shortest dash** and the **smallest circle** that draw cleanly without skipping, and say whether the dots show. Two things the pipeline does, so they are expected: the 0.3 mm dashes come out as one line (finalize joins strokes whose ends are under 0.4 mm apart before the plotter gets them), and a true point never reaches the plotter (the render drops zero-length strokes and finalize any shorter than 0.3 mm), so the dots are the shortest strokes that do.
- **Ink crossings** (black sheet: Signo gold, silver and Moonlight 10 fl pink; white sheet, sealed: all seven inks; the gold sheet has none): every pair of inks crosses twice, the row's ink across and the column's ink down. The pen plotted later is on top, in the sheet's plot order (see Pens): on the black silver, then fl pink, then gold; on the white carbon (Micron 01), Micron 08, blue, purple, silver, fl pink, fl orange. Say whether any crossing **smears or drags** the earlier ink, and if you plot a sheet a second time with a pause between pens (10 minutes or so), whether waiting helps.
- **Cut ladder** (gold sheet, lower left; cut it with G1, before gluing; its labels are hidden under the black): wedges whose tips close to 60, 45, 30 and 20 degrees; slots 3, 4, 5 and 6 mm wide and 30 long; three windows round a kept island held by one bridge 2, 3 or 4 mm wide (as the shirt cut holds the tie at its knot and tip); a notch open to the bottom trim. Find the **sharpest wedge** whose tip cuts clean, the **narrowest slot** that cuts clean, the **narrowest bridge** that holds its island, and whether the notch cuts clean at the trim.
- **Edge rulers** (each sheet, the middle of each side; the white's and gold's are hidden once glued): four short lines 12, 13, 14 and 16 mm from the paper edge, labelled, that is 1, 2, 3 and 5 mm inside the crop line (all art is clipped to the crop line, so the margin itself cannot carry lines). Before trimming, measure with a rule from the paper edge to the 12 line on each side: the difference from 12 mm is how far the plot landed from where it was placed on the bed.
- **Verniers** (read to 0.1 mm, with a loupe): there are four, two per neighbouring pair of sheets. Black over gold at W1 and gold over white at G1 each have an **x** vernier on the window's bottom edge (it reads left-right registration) and a **y** vernier on its right edge (it reads up-down registration). Each has a main scale of 21 ticks at 1.00 mm on the lower sheet (10 mm either side of its 0 tick, every fifth tick longer, running 4 mm under the upper paper; on the gold in black ink for W1, on the white in carbon for G1) and a vernier of 11 ticks at 0.90 mm on the upper sheet's paper, starting at the edge (on the black in silver for W1, on the gold in black ink for G1). The two 0 ticks line up when registration is perfect. The main scales of the G verniers are on the white, under the gold: read them on the loose sheet before gluing, or through G1 after.
  - Find the vernier tick that continues in a straight line across the cut into a main-scale tick. Call its number k: 0 is the vernier's first tick, 10 its last, ticks 5 and 10 are longer.
  - The main-scale tick at or just before the vernier's 0 tick, counted from the main 0 tick, gives the whole millimetres, n. The vernier tick k that lines up gives the tenths.
  - Reading = n + 0.1 x k mm. The arrow marked + is the positive direction: positive means the upper sheet sits further right (x) or further down (y) than the lower one. Example: the vernier's 0 tick falls just past the main 0 tick and its tick 3 lines up: +0.3 mm. If the vernier's 0 tick falls just before the main 0 tick, n is -1: with tick 7 lined up the reading is -1 + 0.7 = -0.3 mm. The tenths can be read for shifts from about -10 mm to +2 mm; beyond that, report just the whole millimetres.

## Report back

- Line width per ink per paper: reads / weak / no (and the width of the single line if you can measure it).
- The smallest cut-guide variant (A, B, C or D) that is still obvious.
- The margin line the knife spared (0.5, 1.0, 1.5 or 2.0 mm), on the black and on the gold sheet.
- The gap-free bleed line (its label in mm), on the gold ladder (through W1) and the white one (through G1).
- The x and y vernier readings for each pair: black over gold (at W1) and gold over white (at G1). Note whether you read them before or after gluing.
- Whether the ghost shows (the carbon hatch through the gold-yellow paper).
- Font test: the smallest legible size per ink per paper, sans and script (1.5, 2.0, 2.6, 3.5 or 5 mm), and whether the 2.6 mm phrase reads in each ink (above all Moonlight 10 fl pink on white, Signo gold on black and the Micron blacks on gold-yellow: the inks the phrase is drawn in).
- Spacing ladder: the tightest separate spacing per ink per paper, for hatch, doubles and triples.
- Dots, dashes and curves: the shortest clean dash and the smallest clean circle per ink per paper, and whether the dots show.
- Crossings: any smear or drag (which pair, which way), and whether a pause between pens helps.
- Cut ladder: the sharpest clean wedge, the narrowest clean slot, the narrowest bridge that held, and the notch.
- Edge rulers: the measured distance from the paper edge to the 12 mm line on each side (top, bottom, left, right), per sheet.

Nothing is plotted or cut until you say go.
